author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Referred to the interior section: draft rules reorganising the Paris National Guard. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Paris National Guard reorganisation debated in Council. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Renvoyé à la section de l'intérieur un projet de règlement pour la réorganisation de la garde nationale parisienne.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Whereas Brigade Chief Dupuy, dead arms in hand at Cairo, commanded the 32nd through five campaigns. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Dupuy died commanding the 32nd through five campaigns: honored. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Considérant que le chef de brigade Dupuy, mort les armes à la main au Caire, a commandé pendant cinq campagnes la 32e demi-brigade.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am satisfied with your conduct in the 8th division. Enlighten the people; let all citizens feel that parties and strife are past. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Parties are over: enlighten the people, set everything in motion. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis satisfait de la conduite que vous tenez dans la 8e division. Éclairez le peuple, faites sentir à tous les citoyens que le temps des partis et des déchirements est passé.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tell me Pichegru's conduct abroad since 18 Fructidor Year V. Truth is wanted, not calumny. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Truth not calumny: what did Pichegru do abroad since Fructidor? Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis chargé de vous demander quelle a été la conduite de Pichegru en pays étranger, depuis le 18 fructidor an V. C'est la vérité qu'on veut connaître, et non la calomnie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You asked 15,000 men. Consul Bonaparte charges me to answer by extraordinary courier. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: 15,000 men demanded and more: courier extraordinary. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous avez demandé 15,000 hommes. Le Consul Bonaparte vient de recevoir votre lettre et me charge de vous écrire par courrier extraordinaire.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Chouan bands gather in Orne. The First Consul complains of hearing nothing from you. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Chouan bands in Orne: what are you doing, what are your troops doing? Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Des rassemblements de chouans existent dans le département de l'Orne. Le Premier Consul se plaint de n'avoir pas encore entendu parler de vous.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The war minister will report at once the clothing administration's state. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Report at once: clothing, linen, shoes, harness administration. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le ministre de la guerre me fera connaître le plus tôt possible l'état actuel de l'administration de l'habillement.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The First Consul saw with indignation chouans settled at Saint-Jean de Margon. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Chouans at Saint-Jean: indignation that Ramefroy's letter sufficed. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le Premier Consul a vu avec indignation qu'on ait laissé établir les chouans à Saint-Jean de Margon.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order General Gardanne and all England-army officers embarked by the 24th. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: England army officers to embark by the 24th, no delay. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Vous ordonnerez sur-le-champ au général de division Gardanne et aux autres officiers de l'armée d'Angleterre d'être rendus le 24 du courant.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “We expect at each moment 1,500,000 francs drawn from Holland, which will be forwarded to you. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Massena from Paris, 1800-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “This hymn must coatain things applicable to all the circumstances of war, and propound the idea that peace follows in the train of victory. u BONAPARTE.'' It is impossible to read the following letter without feelings of astonishment: […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Lucien Bonaparte from ^ Paris, 1800-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I was very well satisfied with him Shall we have peace } Shall we have war? However this may be, the Emperor treats us with the greatest politeness. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Brune from Paris, 1800-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “that the intention of his Catholic Majesty in leaving fifteen vessels at Brest was not to render them useless to the advantage and glory of the two nations; that consequently the First Consul desires orders may be given to Admiral Gravina by telegraph to second the sortie of the French fleet. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from 7M, 1800-03-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You will inform citizen Otto, the French Commissioner in London, that the Government will consent to the exchange of General Don for Napper Tandy and his companions; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from Paris, 1800-03-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Consuls of the Republic desire you will inform the managers of the different theatres that no dramatic work ought to be accepted without your permission. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Lucien Bonaparte from Paris, 1800-04-05. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “When you receive this letter the gallant army of the East will have re-entered the ports of the Republic after having left in Egypt immortal traces of its glorious works. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Kleber from Paris, 1800-04-19. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “By letters I have received it appears that Desaix, Menou, Davoust, and several other generals of courage were opposed to the evacuation of Egypt. All that I say here is intended for you. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Consuls Of The Republic, Lausanne, 1800-05-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Consuls Of The Republic from Lausanne, 1800-05-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “** We are struggling against ice, snow, storms, and avalanches. The St. Bernard, astonished to see so many persons crossing it, throws obstacles in our way. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Consuls Of The Republic, Martigny, 1800-05-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Consuls Of The Republic from Martigny, 1800-05-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “On the 5 th June, Bonaparte pronounced a long allocution to the clergy of Milan. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Fouchfi from Headquarters, 1800-05-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have just received your letter of the 22nd Floreal. I beg you will have the inclosed printed at length in the official journal, for it is well for the public to know the situation of the army of Egypt when I left it, and how exaggerated are the reports made by the agents of England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Second Italian campaign opens: First Consul writing to his colleagues. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “but how came it that 16,00.0 or 18,000 Frenchmen were afraid of 30,000 Turks? Six thousand men would have been sufficient to have beaten them, captured their guns and camels, &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Moreau from 5M, 1800-05-05. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Marengo, June, 1800. " Soldiers: When we began our march, one department of France was in the hands of the enemy. Consternation pervaded the south of the Repubhc. You advanced. Joy and hope in our country have succeeded to consternation and fear. The enemy, terror - struck, seeks only to regain his frontiers. […]”
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: Marengo eve proclamation.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Field of Marengo, fune, 1800. " Sire: — It is on the field of battle, amid the sufferings of a multitude of wounded, and surrounded by fifteen thousand corpses, that I beseech your Majesty to listen to the voice of humanity, and not to suffer two brave nations to cut each other's throats for interests not their own. […]”
sourceTitle: Letter to the Emperor of Austria, 1800-06-01
archive: Tarbell, Napoleon's Addresses (1897) — public domain translations
context: To Austria, on the field.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall arrive unexpectedly in Paris. It is not my intention to have triumphal arches or any kind of ceremony. I have too good an opinion of myself to care about such nonsense. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Lucien Bonaparte from Lyons, 1800-06-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write to General Kleber that when the news of the capitulation arrived, the Brest squadron was about to sail with 4,000 troops and war stores; that we have only just learned the capitulation has been broken, and that he has reconquered Egypt; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: After Marengo: Kléber, Egypt, and broken capitulations. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “BULLETIN TO THE ARMY. "Milan, izrdjune 1800. 'A Turkish ambassador coming from Leghorn on board an English frigate has arrived at Genoa. He has informed Admiral Keith of the deplorable condition of the Grand Vizier who has been driven back across the desert. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Milan, 1800-06-21. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I beg you will invite two of the best virtuosos to go to Paris in order to sing a duo in Italian at the fete of the 14th July. You will give them all that is necessary for their voyage, &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884), Vol. I — public domain
context: Virtuosos for the 14 July fête — war administration as usual. English from the 1884 Bingham translation (public domain); French in the Second Empire Correspondance.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I congratulate you, General, on the brilliant results of your campaign. We are expecting every moment an answer from Vienna, and if it does not arrive in a few days we shall recommence hostilities in Italy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Moreau from Paris, 1800-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “In the year VIII. (1800) an attempt was made to re-establish the Academy on its ancient footing, and the idea was encouraged by Lucien Bonaparte, then Minister of the Interior. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Lucien Bonaparte from Paris, 1800-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “command of his centre. He has made the most favourable report of your operations. I see by your letter that you are zealous to acquire glory; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Suchet from Paris, 1800-07-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Consuls have been informed that the citizen Foissac-Latour has returned from Austria and dishonours the French uniform by wearing it. Let him know that he ceased to belong to the service of the Republic the day he basely surrendered the citadel of Mantua. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Carnot from Paris, 1800-07-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is my intention to send General Berthier to Spain without any apparent diplomatic title. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from 2Zth, 1800-07-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have already informed you that you have been called by the esteem and confidence of the Consuls to the chief command of the forces in Germany. The modesty with which you refused to accept this important command has proved an additional motive for conferring it upon you. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Moreau from Paris, 1800-08-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “(words omitted). History will not forget this. *' I am not insensible to the misfortunes of your family. (more words omitted). I shall contribute with pleasure to the pleasantness and tranquillity of your retreat. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Comte De Provence, Paris, 1800-09-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Comte De Provence from Paris, 1800-09-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “ablished for the purpose of giving him intelligence that I was to be at Nowly on the 8th and at Chinnoor on the 9th. His majesty was misled by this information, and was nearer me than he expected. […]”
sourceTitle: To To Major Munro, Camp at Yepulpuroy, 1800-09-11
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: India 1800: the other empire rising.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “** The courier who was expected has returned from Vienna, bringing no positive answer. This proves that the Court of Vienna wishes to gain the winter. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Carnot from Paris, 1800-09-13. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I pity those who have not sufficient virtue to second you in your noble resolution, and whose courage has failed them. They will find in France that contempt due to men who, no matter what their services, are deficient in the necessary amount of constancy. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Menou from Paris, 1800-10-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You must show no pity in such cases. If any revolts take place in remote corners, make severe examples. All foreign people but especially Italians require to be dealt with severely from time to time. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Brune from Paris, 1800-11-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I send you the Citizen Jerome Bonaparte to serve his apprenticeship in the marine. You know he will have to be kept in order so as to make up for lost time. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Rear-Admiral Ganteaume from Paris, 1800-11-22. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I should not regret expending 40,000 francs in this affair.BONAPARTE" On the same day Talleyrand was ordered to see that every vessel which tried to reach Egypt carried 1,000 muskets, 10,000 cannon balls, 250 pairs of pistols, 250 sabres, and medical stores. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Chaptal from Paris, 1800-12-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “that we shall evacuate it only on the conclusion of a general peace, and that it is in the interest of the Porte to resume its ancient relations with France. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from Paris, 1800-12-16. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “they counted upon the snow and ice; they were not yet acquainted with you. *' I salute you affectionately, […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Moreau from Paris, 1801-01-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Legislators, the Republic triumphs. Hohenlinden's victory resounded through Europe. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Hohenlinden resounds through Europe. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Législateurs, la République triomphe. La victoire de Hohenlinden a retenti dans toute l'Europe.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The navy minister shall arrest Citizen Tallien, charged with quitting Egypt without passport. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Tallien arrested for quitting Egypt without passport. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le ministre de la marine fera mettre en arrestation le citoyen Tallien, prévenu d'avoir quitté l'Égypte sans passe-port.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Hand M. de Muzquiz a letter complaining of changed preparations against Portugal. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Spain pressed to make Portugal act against England. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de remettre à M. de Muzquiz une lettre dans laquelle vous vous plaindrez des changements dans les préparatifs contre le Portugal.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Write General Menou that no serious Egypt landing can happen but at Aboukir. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Aboukir the only serious landing: warn Menou. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je désire que vous écriviez au général Menou, pour lui faire connaître qu'un débarquement en Égypte ne peut avoir sérieusement lieu qu'à Aboukir.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “to send four ships of the line and two frigates, with 2,000 soldiers, to Trinidad; and to arm all the vessels it possessed at Cadiz, Barcelona, and Carthagena, in order to attack Mahon. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from Paris, 1801-01-07. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I thank you for your news of the extraordinary 3 Nivôse event. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Thanks for Hohenlinden — and the infernal machine survived. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous remercie de ce que vous me dites sur l'événement extraordinaire du 3 nivôse.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Forty men leave Bicêtre tomorrow for Orléans, thence to embark at Nantes. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Forty men from Bicêtre to Orléans to Nantes, then by sea. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Quarante individus partent demain de Bicêtre pour Orléans, et de là se rendront à Nantes, où ils seront embarqués.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Brune putting Tuscany under your orders seems to me extremely wise. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Brune put Tuscany under Murat: wise confidence. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: La mesure prise par le général Brune, de mettre la Toscane sous vos ordres, me paraît extrêmement sage.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “A law will let Ajaccio sell lands to bring water. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Ajaccio may sell lands for water; old forts demolished. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Une loi va autoriser la commune d'Ajaccio à vendre une partie de ses biens pour se procurer de l'eau.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Combis's mission: remind Santo Domingo's people the land is now French. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Combis mission: remind Spanish Santo Domingo it is French. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le principal but de la mission du citoyen Combis à Saint-Domingue est de faire souvenir aux habitants que ce pays est désormais français.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “General Toussaint Louverture, amid revolutionary storms, saved France a great colony by prudence and courage. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Toussaint praised: prudence and courage saved the colony. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le général Toussaint Louverture, au milieu des orages de la révolution, est parvenu, par sa prudence et son courage, à sauver à la France une grande colonie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Draft a treaty for Helvetia to cede all Valais to Brigg. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Valais to the Léman department: treaty with Helvetia. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de préparer un projet de traité avec l'Helvétie, pour qu'elle nous cède tout le Valais jusqu'à Brigg.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Yesterday a Russian courier arrived in fifteen days with an extremely friendly letter. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: A friendly Russian letter in fifteen days: Paul melts. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Hier est arrivé de Russie un courrier qui a fait la route en quinze jours; il m'a apporté une lettre extrêmement amicale.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They must stir themselves at Madrid. Make the z 2 340 thp: correspondence of napoleon. Spaniards feel how shameful it is for the Spanish monarchy that two vessels should blockade seven in the port of Cadiz. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from ■' Paris, 1801-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It will be remarked that Portugal, instead of 8,000,000, was now called upon to pay from 15,000,000 to 20,000,000 francs. It becomes difficult to follow all the territorial combinations in which the First Consul indulged. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from I'^Th, 1801-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am going to assemble, as your Majesty appears to wish, 300 or 400 gun launches in the ports of Flanders, where I shall concentrate an army. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Emperor Of Russia, I'jth, 1801-02-01
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Emperor Of Russia from I'Jth, 1801-02-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Dispatch a night courier to General Murat, reaching Foligno tomorrow. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Night courier to Murat at Foligno: Rome instructions. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie d'expédier dans la nuit un courrier au général Murat, qui arrive demain à Foligno.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “but on the condition of the Spaniards giving us three of the frigates at Barcelona or Carthagena, and six of the line of battle ships at the Havannah. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from Paris, 1801-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Send Madrid the great interest I take in Spain's navy acting again. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Spain must make its navy act: recapitulatory dispatch. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Expédiez un courrier à l'ambassadeur à Madrid; vous lui récapitulerez le grand intérêt que j'attache à voir les Espagnols reprendre de l'activité.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Brigade Chief Savary rides post-haste to Lorient. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858), Vols. VI–VII — public domain (French)
context: Savary rides post-haste to Lorient for the Anacreon. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le chef de brigade Savary partira en toute diligence pour se rendre à Lorient.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “<< BONAPARTE." Maury, of lamp-post fame, the inventor of the appellation sans culottes was at that moment acting as agent for Louis XVIII. at the Papal Court. He soon afterwards became the devoted adherent of Bonaparte, and remained devoted until 18 14. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from Paris, 1801-03-12. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order Brigadier-General Houdetot to start immediately for Rochefort. Give the same order to two or three officers who can fix public attention on the proposed expedition […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Forfait from Paris, 1801-03-13. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He was not then aware that the maritime confederation had experienced two fatal blows, and that the Russian alliance was at an end, owing to the death of Paul, and Nelson's victory in the Baltic. […]”

context: Letter to The King Of Spain from St. Cloud, 1802-11-27. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Piedmont's church affairs need settling. If France has a bishop per two departments, six may stay in Piedmont. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Six bishops suffice Piedmont, endowed with all Church goods. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est instant d'arranger les affaires ecclésiastiques du Piémont. S'il n'y a en France qu'un évêque par deux départements, il n'y a pas d'inconvénient à laisser en Piémont six évêques.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Report on wood-cutting bills as paper money. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Wood-cuttings as paper money: 100 to 10,000 francs. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le Premier Consul désire que vous fassiez un rapport sur les traites de coupes de bois à organiser comme papier-monnaie.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Only germinal/messidor wood payments fund Year XI; the rest Year XII. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Wood revenues split Year XI/XII by month of falling due. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Mon intention est de n'affecter au service de l'an XI, sur la coupe des bois, que les payements qui échoient en germinal et en messidor.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Tell General Brune to demand instant restitution of Citizen Ruffin's ship, seized by Djezzar-Pasha. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Djezzar seized Ruffin's rich ship: demand it back at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de faire connaître au général Brune qu'il ait à réclamer que le bâtiment du citoyen Ruffin, confisqué par Djezzar-Pacha, lui soit sur-le-champ restitué.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Duroc gives Beauvoisin all his Ambigu plus the Ivernois pamphlet. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Beauvoisin gets the Ambigu plus Ivernois pamphlet: write up England. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le citoyen Duroc fera connaître au citoyen Beauvoisin qu'il m'adresse tout ce qu'il a de l'Ambigu, ainsi que le pamphlet d'Ivernois.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Ré, Oléron and Sainte-Marguerite must hold all sentenced deportees. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Ré, Oléron, Sainte-Marguerite organised for deportees. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Il est indispensable d'organiser aux îles de Ré, d'Oléron et Sainte-Marguerite, des prisons pour y renfermer tous les individus condamnés à la déportation.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Deputies, your fatherland is critical. Moderation, prudence, sacrificed passions alone can save it. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Switzerland critical: moderation, prudence, sacrifice of passions. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Citoyens Députés, la situation de votre patrie est critique. La modération, la prudence et le sacrifice de vos passions sont nécessaires pour la sauver.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order plans for Quiberon, Belle-Île and Boulogne batteries. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Plans for Quiberon, Belle-Île, Marcouf, Boulogne works. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de donner ordre de dresser des plans pour mettre le fort Quiberon, la place de Belle-Île et les batteries de Boulogne en état.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “They are the tyrants of India; they are suspicious and jealous; the Captain-General must act with gentleness, dissimulation, and simplicity. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Rear-Admiral Decres from 15/A, 1803-01-15. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Read the enclosed report. 'Liquidation of newly created pensions' means nothing to me. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: 'Liquidation of newly created pensions' means nothing: explain. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie de prendre connaissance du rapport ci-joint. Je ne conçois pas ce que veut dire ce mot de liquidation des pensions nouvellement créées.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The 1,200 sailed from Havre, Dunkerque ready, three Toulon expeditions: troops arriving together. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Havre, Dunkerque, Toulon, Genoa, Corsica sail together. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Les 1,200 hommes qui sont partis du Havre, ceux prêts à partir de Dunkerque, les trois expéditions parties de Toulon feront arriver à la fois un assez grand nombre de troupes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Glad of Fort Dauphin retaken; take directly my full confidence and approval of vigorous measures. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Fort Dauphin retaken with pleasure: full confidence, vigorous measures approved. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: J'ai vu avec plaisir la reprise du fort Dauphin; je veux directement vous assurer de l'entière confiance que le Gouvernement a en vous.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Fifteen thousand men shipped or shipping to Saint-Domingue. Combine now a 6,500 expedition. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: 15,000 men shipped; combine now a 6,500 expedition. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Quinze mille hommes viennent ou vont finir d'être expédiés à Saint-Domingue. Mais il faut combiner, dès aujourd'hui, une expédition de 6,500 hommes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Order the Brisgau commander to receive two Austrian companies. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Two Austrian companies into Brisgau: no obstacle. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je vous prie d'ordonner au commandant dans le Brisgau de recevoir deux compagnies de troupes autrichiennes.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My trust in your great talents bids me ask an elementary mathematics work for the national lycées. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: The great mineralogist to write the lycées' math textbook. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: La confiance que j'ai dans vos grands talents me porte à désirer que vous vous chargiez de faire un ouvrage élémentaire pour la classe de mathématiques des Lycées nationaux.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The nègre Télémaque thanks the First Consul for the Cap mayoralty, protesting devotion to the Republic. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Black mayor thanks and devotion: recommend this brave nègre. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Le nègre Télémaque remercie le Premier Consul de l'avoir nommé maire du Cap. Il proteste de son dévouement à la République.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Madame de Staël, forbidden Paris, reaches Melun the 20th. Order police to turn her straight back. […]”
archive: Correspondance de Napoléon Ier, Second Empire ed. (Paris, 1858) — public domain (French)
context: Staël forbidden Paris, arrives at Melun: turn her back at once. Translated for Chronicle from the public-domain French; original below.
originalText: Je suis instruit que madame de Staël, malgré la défense qui lui a été faite de venir à Paris, arrive le 20 à Melun. Donnez ordre de la faire sur-le-champ rétrograder.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “' 7 Constantine, tell him that I regret he did not come to Paris. You will speak to the Empress of the pleasure I experienced on seeing her uncle here, and how he amused himself in Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Brigadier Colbert from Paris, 1803-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “« BONAPARTE." You will know much better than I can tell you how this emigrant duke has been courted by Buonaparte, through his minister in Russia. We must recollect that he is a Frenchman, and his ultimate views probably turn to getting back some of his estates in France. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Paris, 1803-03-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Your letter reached me at the Malmaison. I desire that the conference should not degenerate into a conversation. Show yourself cold, haughty, and even somewhat proud. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Amiens ruptured: the truce is over, the invasion army rises.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “if the note does not contain this word, make him insert it, remarking that we must really know whereabout we are, and that we are weary of this state of uncertainty. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from St. Cloud, 1803-05-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “ugh I am aware that generally speaking it is better to keep the sick men with their corps; but in a case of this kind, where there are so many men sick, and the carriage for the sick is so insufficient, and there is every probability that there will be more sick, […]”
sourceTitle: To To Col St venson, Poonah, 1803-05-02
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Poona 1803: subsidiary alliances.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the different letters which it has pleased your majesty to write to me. Circumstances become more and more serious, and war is about to be rekindled between France and England. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Prince Regent Of Portugal, St.  Cloud, 1803-05-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Prince Regent Of Portugal from St. Cloud, 1803-05-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “25,000 francs to M. Chatillon; 30,000 to the Bishop of Orleans, and 25,000 to the Prefect of the Loire-Inferieure. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Regnier from St. Cloud, 1803-06-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have directed this general to make the army defile with the honours of war, to disarm it, to dismount the cavalry, and to send it prisoner to France. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from 19M, 1803-06-19. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter, good little Josephine. I perceived with sorrow that you suffered from the journey. But a few days of repose will do much for you, I am very well, indeed. I went yesterday to the hunt at Marly,1 and wounded myself very slightly in one finger, in shooting a boar. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Malmaison summer: health anxieties.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I recommend you to be inflexible as regards its execution, and not to permit the introduction of any English goods or couriers. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Mortier from ■Bruges, 1803-07-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received your letter of the 29th of June. You do not speak of your health, or of the effect of the baths. I see that you intend to be on your return in eight days. That will afford great pleasure to your friend, who wearies of being alone. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: 29 June letter answered; health unwritten.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “to France as a minister, by procuring the liberation of the territory in 18 18, at an earlier date than that originally fixed by the allies. The chambers voted him 2,000/. a year, but the Duke — although his pecuniary circumstances were anything but brilliant — refused to accept the pension. […]”
sourceTitle: To The Right Hon. Henry Addington, lUh, 1803-07-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The Right Hon. Henry Addington from Luh, 1803-07-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “War has not yet been declared, but the conduct of the ambassador, acting on the orders of his government, necessitates precautions. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Lady Hamilton from Amphion, 1803-07-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The affairs of Ireland make me' feel the necessity of your having some private conferences with the chiefs of the United Irishmen now in Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Flotilla orders: flatboats, tides, Boulogne.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I shall arrive at St. Cloud when least expected, perhaps during the night. The next day I shall receive the authorities. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Consul Cambacirils from Namur, 1803-08-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “You can offer them 25,000 men, 40,000 muskets, with artillery and ammunition, and assure them that the Government will undertake not to make peace with England until the independence of Ii-eland has been proclaimed; provided that 20,000 United Irishmen join the French army on its landing. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Rear-Admiral Decres from Sedan, 1803-08-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The most important matter with regard to our relations with Spain is not the question of subsidies; it is not the execution of the treaty by which we are bound, but it is — 1st, The strange conduct of having allowed two vessels anchored at Algesiras to be cut out, and not offering an indemnity. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from St. Cloud, 1803-08-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think it will be useful to send the last note from Russia to Laforest. He can communicate it to M. de Haugwitz, pointing out all its absurdity. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from St. Cloud, 1803-08-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Gentlemen, — I sent to offer the French Admiral in Toulon an exchange of prisoners. After keeping the boat waiting three hours, a message come down that the French Admiral would receive no letter or message, therefore you must blame the cruelty of your own Admiral for keeping you prisoners. […]”
sourceTitle: To The French Officers Prisoners Of War At, off  Toulon, 1803-08-10
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to The French Officers Prisoners Of War At from Off Toulon, 1803-08-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I return you the despatch from Madrid of the 13th Fructidor. I am surprised that we have no other news. Make out a list of all the complaints we have against Spain, so that we may have materials ready in the event of requiring them.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Invasion diplomacy between reviews.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “and if so, whether in the event of their coming to Syria or Egypt they will be secured from pillage and looked upon as friends. Our agent must endeavour to procure information with regard to the force and situation of this new sect. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from Izth, 1803-09-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “If this be the case I beg you will withdraw it, for the troops will fall ill. Should the English attempt an attack on the Isle of Walcheren you will have time to succour it. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Davoust from 2Zth, 1803-09-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I am informed. Citizen Minister, that Madame de Stael has arrived at Maffiers. Let her be informed through one of her friends, without making a scandal, that if on the 8th she has not taken her departure she shall be escorted to the frontier by the gendarmery. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Regnier from Paris, 1803-10-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is not my intention no matter what the pretext, to allow this ridiculous pretension to exist. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from St. Cloud, 1803-10-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “It is time for you to propose the formation of the Irish battalions. I wish you to hand me a return of the Irish who are here, and who count upon joining the expedition, to settle their rank, &c. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Paris, 1803-11-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have ordered them to be settled, my intention being, under no circumstances, to borrow money from the bank. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Perregaux from Paris, 1803-11-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “" I know that several comedies appropriate to the circumstance have been presented. A choice should be made so that they may be played in the various theatres of Paris, and especially at the camps of Boulogne, Bruges, and other places where the army is quartered. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Chaptal from Paris, 1803-11-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I return you your despatches, Citizen Minister. Tell Citizen Laforest that I have read his despatch with great interest. It will be well to warn the Turkish ambassador that the English, who evidently encourage the Beys, intend to seize upon Egypt.”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: From the invasion camp.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Citizen General, — I have received your letter, and have given orders for hoods to be served out to all the men forming part of the expedition to Ireland, of which you shall have the command. Affairs are settled with Spain and Portugal. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Boulogne camps: invasion of England prepared.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “He was made a senator in 1805, a count in 1809, a peer by the Bourbons in 1814, a commander of the Order of St. Louis in 18 16, a marshal the same year, and a marquis in 18 17. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Augereau from Boulogne, 1803-11-12. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The solution of this problem offers such immense advantages that it is improbable anything reasonable can have been imagined by a Swiss mountaineer. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from 17/A, 1803-11-17. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Let Madame Bourmont be examined as to the foreigner who paid her a visit a month ago. Let. her understand that the result of her examination may have important consequences, and that she ought to tell the truth clearly. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Regnier from Paris, 1803-12-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I have received the letter in which you announce the arrival of forty sail in the Somme. I have also received the report of the visit made to the Prince de Galles. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Admiral Bruix from Paris, 1803-12-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “that I know everything; that the brothers Bertin are paid by England, as is proved by the tone of their articles; that it is my intention to allow only those journals which excite the nation against England and encourage it to support the vicissitudes of war, to exist. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Regnier from -Zgth, 1803-12-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “de Coucy, the ex-Bishop of La Rochelle, is in Spain, where he is behaving very badly. His incendiary pastorals encourage the civil war in La Vendue. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Talleyrand from Paris, 1803-12-12. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My Friend, — I have not received any news from you for several days; I should, however, have been glad to know what effect the waters have had, and how you pass your time. I have been here for the last week, and intend going to-morrow to Boulogne. […]”
sourceTitle: To Josephine, Nivose 1804 (revolutionary date; day approximate)
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Nivôse Year XII: no news for days. Revolutionary calendar date; rendered to the 1st, marked approximate.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The message naturally contained the most terrible invectives against England. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Paris, 1804-01-04. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Citizen Tascher, officer of the Guard, you will start to-morrow for Rome. You will alight at the residence of Cardinal Fesch, Ambassador of the Republic, who will present you to the Pope, into whose hands you will deliver the inclosed letter. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Tascher.I from 13M, 1804-01-13. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Let him be sent to the first French posts at Rimini, and conveyed under escort to Paris. No attention should be paid to the steps taken by the Russians, because they have not been approved of by the Emperor. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Cardinal Fesch from Paris, 1804-01-13. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The idea is to hand over this portfolio, into which the First Consul will put all the information he wishes to be beheved. But in order that a great importance should be attached to this portfolio, at least 50,000/. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Citizen Regnier from 24M, 1804-01-24. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “For the last week we have been in pursuit of forty brigands composed of Georges and his band, who disembarked at three different places. Another band is to disembark; we have arrested all the men who were to make signals. Savary awaits them at Biville. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Camp of Boulogne: Soult drills the invasion army.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “that the King of England would not sanction any exchange without appending unusual and arbitrary conditions. It is my intention that no flag of truce should be received at Toulon. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Rear-Admiral Decres from Paris, 1804-03-02. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Duke of Wellington
displayText: “A Public Man's Duty. It is necessary for a man who fills a public situation, and who has great public interests in charge, to lay aside all private considerations, whether on his own account or that of other persons.”
archive: Wellington, Despatches 1799–1815 (1902 selection) — public domain
context: Poona 1804: Mahratta wars.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The Due d'Enghien is to be taken to the castle of Vincennes, where arrangements have been made for his reception. The First Consul desires that the name of this prisoner, and everything concerning him, may be kept secret. he travels under the name of Plessis. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection (London, 1884), Vols. II–III — public domain
context: Murat governs Paris as the Enghien crisis breaks.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “". You will also order General Caulaincourt to go to Offenburg with 200 dragoons, to surround 'the town, and to arrest the Baroness de Reich and other English agents. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Berthier from Paris, 1804-03-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “The First Consul desires that the name of this prisoner, and everything concerning him, may be kept secret. he travels under the name of Plessis. " BONAPARTE." The commandant of Vincennes was also ordered to keep everything a profound secret. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Murat from La Malmaison, 1804-03-10. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “receive their complaints, inspect their arms, and make sure that they want for nothing. There is a great advantage in holding these inspections of seven or eight hours; […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to General Marmont from La Malmaison, 1804-03-12. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Madame and dear Sister,— I have learned with pain that you have not the good sense to conform to the manners and customs of the city of Rome; that you show contempt for the inhabitants, and that your eyes are unceasingly turned towards Paris. […]”
archive: Bingham, Selection from the Letters and Despatches (London, 1884) — public domain
context: Letter to Pauline Borghese from Paris, 1804-04-01. Full text in the Bingham selection (public domain).

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “Madam and dear Wife, — For the last four days since I have been absent from you I have been constantly on horseback, and this exercise has not impaired my health. " M. author: Napoleon Bonaparte

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “My love, I have been at Calais since midnight. I think of setting out this evening for Dunkirk. I am satisfied with what I see, and am in very good health. I hope that the waters may benefit you, as much as the bustle, the sight of camps, and the ocean have me. Eugene has gone to Blois. […]”
archive: Confidential Correspondence of Napoleon and Josephine (London, 1856) — public domain
context: Calais: setting out for Dunkirk this evening.

author: Napoleon Bonaparte
displayText: “I think it necessary to mention this, in order that you may no longer be the dupe of his assumed openness. Talleyrand was then ordered to draw up a note complaining of the conduct of Russia, and the tone of the despatches received from St. […]”
